chapters.title: The Polarity Strategy: Declare War on Your Enemies

chapterBreakdown.gentle: Talia knew something was wrong before she admitted what it was. A reorganization plan kept getting presented as neutral housekeeping, yet each version made another leader stronger by making her team smaller. That is the chapter's first lesson. Some conflicts are real even when the language around them stays polite. Greene's move is not to cultivate hostility. It is to stop calling structural opposition a misunderstanding just because the sharper label feels unpleasant. An enemy, in this narrow sense, is the person whose position improves when yours weakens. Once you see that, you stop giving away information, access, and timing to the wrong person. The reversal matters just as much. If you start treating every critic or tense peer as an enemy, the move collapses into paranoia and damages the relationships that actually build your life. It sharpens judgment without inventing enemies everywhere.
chapterBreakdown.direct: Talia's meeting reveals the chapter's mechanism cleanly. Another division head keeps using calm, institutional language while advancing a plan that only works if her team disappears. The useful question is not whether he seems mean. The useful question is whether his gain depends on her loss. That is Greene's definition in practice. The strategy asks you to identify real opposition before you leak strength through naive access, candor, or delay. It does not ask you to act combative for its own sake. The payoff is cleaner judgment: you share less with the wrong person, read repeated moves as a pattern, and stop mistaking etiquette for safety. The limit is nonnegotiable. If you use the label everywhere, you turn ordinary tension into false conflict and poison collaboration. The right move is classification first, then narrower disclosure, steadier timing, and cleaner boundaries with actual collaborators.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: Talia was not being attacked with raised voices. She was being narrowed out of the room by someone whose plan got stronger as her team disappeared. That is why the chapter starts here. Real opposition rarely announces itself in a way that flatters your instincts. It often arrives dressed as process, alignment, and mature professionalism. The move is to name the incentive structure before it names you. If another person's upside depends on your weakened position, stop briefing them like an ally. Stop reading the pattern as bad luck. That is the gain. The risk runs the other way: once you start calling every disagreement a threat, you get sloppy, suspicious, and alone. The chapter rewards cold accuracy, not theatrical aggression, and it punishes readers who confuse vigilance with paranoia fast. The point is precision under pressure, not living in a permanent war posture.

easy.oneMinuteRecap: The chapter asks one thing first: who actually gains when you lose ground? Name that structure honestly, then guard your access and timing without turning every tense relationship into a war.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Talia did not need a dramatic betrayal to understand what was happening. She needed one clean reading of incentives. A reorganization proposal kept returning in slightly revised forms, each one framed as efficiency and each one ending with her team absorbed elsewhere. The other division head stayed cordial enough that she kept wanting to give the plan a softer explanation. That hesitation is the pressure point Greene goes after. People often refuse to name real opposition because the sharper reading feels rude, anxious, or excessive.

The chapter narrows the idea of enemy so it can actually help. It is not the person who annoys you, questions you, or once competed with you. It is the person whose improvement is tied in a concrete way to your reduced position. That can be a rival in a promotion process, a counterparty in a negotiation, a litigant, a grant competitor, or an internal operator whose budget case strengthens if your scope shrinks. Once that structure is visible, the right behavior changes. You stop briefing them as if interests are shared. You stop confusing access with goodwill.

Greene's useful contribution is the insistence that etiquette and safety are not the same thing. A person can speak gently, praise collaboration, and still be working a pattern that leaves you exposed. The chapter matters because readers often lose to that mismatch. They keep relabeling repeated moves as accidental friction and only recognize the conflict after they have given away timing, candor, and room.

But the reversal is just as important. Soraya nearly misread a studio classmate as an enemy because the criticism was public and the pressure was high. Once the assignment structure changed, the shared incentive became obvious. That is the chapter's warning. Anxiety loves enemy stories because they simplify ambiguity. The strategy only works when the evidence is structural. Used lazily, it turns criticism into betrayal and tension into paranoia.

So the operating rule is narrow. Ask who benefits if you weaken, what pattern keeps repeating, and what changes if you withhold access. If the answers point to real opposition, adjust. If not, do not force the frame. The gain is clarity. The price of careless use is isolation.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Talia's case makes the chapter concrete. A division head keeps presenting consolidation plans in neutral language, but every version improves his position by shrinking hers. That is the signal the chapter cares about. Enemy status is not about warmth, bluntness, or personal chemistry. It is about an incentive structure in which your loss feeds someone else's gain.

This is why Greene pushes the reader to name opposition directly. If you refuse to use the sharper label, you act from the wrong map. You keep sharing plans with the person building a case against you. You hand over context, drafts, and timing because you want the situation to be friendlier than it is. Later, when the move lands, you call it surprise. The surprise was often self-authored.

The chapter also draws a line between conflict and mood. A critic is not automatically an enemy. A blunt peer is not automatically an enemy. A competitor is not automatically an enemy if the incentives can still align. The useful test is concrete: does this person's position improve if mine degrades? If the answer is yes in a meaningful way, stop treating the relationship as if interests are shared. Shift what you disclose, document more carefully, and stop explaining away repeated patterns.

Talia's correction is instructive because it is not dramatic. She does not perform outrage. She tightens access, builds her case upward, and stops assuming advance warning will come from the other side. That is what naming opposition buys: better judgment and fewer leaks.

The reversal keeps the strategy from becoming stupid. Soraya starts reading a studio classmate as hostile because the criticism is public and her nerves are hot. Then the incentive structure changes and the supposed enemy turns out to be part of the same outcome. That is the trap. If you label every tense relationship as opposition, you lose collaboration, accuracy, and trust at the same time. The strategy is useful only when it is earned by structure rather than emotion.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Talia kept wanting to believe the slide deck was just process. It was not. Another division head was using institutional language to make his budget case stronger by making her team disappear. That is the chapter's first cut. Opposition often arrives in the exact tone that makes you hesitate to call it what it is.

Greene's move is harsh because it rejects that hesitation. If another person's gain is materially tied to your loss, stop pretending you are reading the same map. That does not require anger. It requires classification. Once the classification is right, the behavior changes fast. You stop feeding someone with drafts, context, and early warnings. You stop handing them the raw material for your own narrowing. And you stop letting courtesy talk you out of defensive intelligence.

Readers usually fail here for a simple reason: the softer story protects their self-image. It feels better to say the conflict is a misunderstanding than to say someone benefits from your stalled progress. But the softer story is expensive. It makes you late. It makes you candid with the wrong audience. It makes you interpret a pattern of small moves as random noise until the larger move is already closing around you.

Talia's recovery is quiet and therefore useful. She does not accuse. She stops leaking. She builds documentation, changes who gets access, and shifts her effort toward people whose incentives are not lined up against her. That is the practical value of enemy recognition. It sharpens allocation.

The reversal is the safeguard against becoming ridiculous. Soraya almost turns studio pressure into a war story because public criticism feels personal. But once the project structure changes, the supposed enemy is tied to her outcome. If you cannot tell the difference between rivalry, discomfort, and real opposition, you will torch allies and call it strength. The chapter rewards a colder standard. Read repeated incentives. Watch the gain map. Then decide who deserves distance and who merely deserves better boundaries. early.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Talia's reorganization meeting looks ordinary at first, which is why it works as the chapter's opening pressure scene. No one insults her. No one announces a vendetta. Another division head keeps presenting a sequence of tidy organizational fixes, each one dressed in the language of alignment and each one ending with her unit smaller, weaker, or easier to absorb. Her delay does not come from lack of intelligence. It comes from a moral hesitation. The sharper reading feels ugly, so she keeps reaching for a gentler explanation.

That hesitation is the real target of the chapter. Greene is arguing that readers often lose not because they cannot fight, but because they refuse to classify the situation correctly. Enemy, in this chapter, is a structural term. It names the person whose position is strengthened by your loss of position. That may be a rival in a promotion lane, a grant competitor, a litigant, a negotiator, a campaign opponent, or an internal operator who needs your scope to contract so theirs can expand. None of that requires melodrama. It only requires a realistic accounting of incentives.

The gain from that accounting is immediate. Once the relationship is named accurately, you stop behaving as if interests are shared. You tighten what you disclose. You notice repeated moves as a pattern rather than as a string of harmless incidents. You stop using civility as evidence. That last point matters. Civility can coexist with real opposition. In fact, modern conflict often depends on that coexistence. The person working against you may benefit from looking mature, measured, and institutionally minded while they narrow your room through process, documentation, or timing.

This is why late recognition is expensive. Readers who soften the label tend to overshare in the name of trust, wait in the name of fairness, and explain away patterns in the name of balance. By the time they accept that the interests were opposed all along, the other side has already gathered context, shaped the room, and defined the tempo. Their innocence was not moral superiority. It was poor classification.

But the chapter gets dangerous if the classification standard drops too low. Soraya's studio case shows the failure mode. Public criticism under pressure can feel indistinguishable from hostility when the nervous system wants a simple enemy story. Yet the incentive structure in her case is shared. The project still rises or falls jointly. If she forces the enemy frame anyway, she converts tension into self-sabotage and damages a collaboration she actually needs.

That is the hard question the chapter has to preserve: what evidence justifies the label? Hurt feelings do not. Status discomfort does not. A sharp peer does not. The chapter earns its force only when the evidence is structural, repeated, and materially consequential. If this person's success still depends on your competent performance, the frame is probably wrong. If your decline clearly improves their position, the softer frame is probably costly.

So the strategy demands a double discipline. First, do not lie to yourself when real opposition exists. Second, do not reward your own anxiety by calling every hard interaction a war. Name the relationship by incentives, adjust disclosure accordingly, and keep the label rare enough that it still means something. Chapter 2 then complicates the picture further. Even once the opponent is named correctly, you can still lose by assuming the current conflict works like the last one you survived.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Talia's meeting matters because it shows how real opposition often hides in normal organizational speech. Another division head keeps proposing consolidation plans that look neutral on the page and consistently improve his position by shrinking hers. The move against her is not loud. It is administrative. That forces the chapter's main distinction. Enemy status is not established by hostility, tone, or personality. It is established by an incentive structure in which your reduced position materially benefits the other side.

Greene's point is that readers often refuse to make that classification because the classification feels impolite. They would rather describe the conflict as process friction, a misunderstanding, or personality noise. That softer description protects their self-image, but it produces bad behavior. They keep disclosing drafts and reasoning to someone who is not using the information for a shared outcome. They keep granting access because they are still acting from the assumption of aligned interests.

The operational value of the chapter is therefore diagnostic before it is tactical. If another person's gains are fed by your losses, stop treating the relationship as neutral. Change disclosure. Document more carefully. Notice the pattern of moves rather than excusing each move in isolation. Modern opposition often works through repeatable small advantages, not dramatic attacks. That is why polite environments can still be dangerous. The other side may prefer process because process conceals intent while still producing effect.

Talia's correction is useful because it stays disciplined. She does not jump to public confrontation. She stops making one error in classification, and that change reorganizes the next set of choices. She no longer briefs the other division head as if their interests are shared. She builds upward, guards timing, and works from the assumption that advance warning will not come from the person whose upside depends on her contraction. The chapter is less about emotional heat than about reducing avoidable leaks.

The reversal prevents the strategy from becoming stupid. Soraya mistakes public criticism in studio for enemy action because public criticism activates threat quickly. But when the incentive structure is inspected, the relationship is still joint. The project outcome is shared. In that setting the enemy label would not sharpen judgment. It would deform it. The cost would be damaged cooperation and a distorted reading of the room.

That is the hard boundary. Structural evidence earns the label. Discomfort does not. One-off rivalry does not. Strong criticism does not. If this person's improvement clearly rides on your degraded standing, the chapter applies. If the outcome still depends on you succeeding together, the chapter probably does not. Readers have to hold both risks at once: late naming leaves them exposed, early or lazy naming leaves them isolated.

So the chapter is really about map discipline. Misclassify the relationship and every later move becomes weaker. Classify it correctly and even simple actions, such as withholding a draft or changing who gets context first, become more effective. The next chapter adds a second pressure test. After naming real opposition, can you see the current conflict clearly enough to avoid fighting it with a dead playbook?
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Talia nearly lost because the move against her looked respectable. A division head kept wrapping the same land grab in the language of alignment, efficiency, and mature process. Every version of the plan left him bigger and her team smaller. No villain speech, no obvious insult, just a clean incentive structure hiding inside civilized language. That is why Greene starts here. Readers do not usually lose because the other side is invisible. They lose because they keep insisting on a softer label than the evidence deserves.

This chapter sets a brutal standard. Enemy does not mean irritating person. It does not mean critic. It does not mean ambitious peer. It means someone whose upside is materially improved by your loss of room, position, credibility, budget, or timing. Once that condition is true, stop behaving like you are inside a shared-interest relationship. Stop handing over the draft, the context, the early warning, and the explanatory goodwill that only make the other side sharper.

The chapter is harsh because politeness is expensive when it becomes misclassification. Readers like the softer story because it lets them feel generous, balanced, and above the conflict. Meanwhile the other side is building a case, shaping the room, or collecting the access they need. Most blindsides are not lightning strikes. They are slow constructions made possible by information the losing side kept donating under the wrong interpretation.

Talia's recovery is instructive because it is not loud. She changes the file, not the theater. She stops briefing the other side into her own narrowing. She documents more, routes context upward, and works from the assumption that the person benefiting from her weakened position will not rescue her from the consequences. That is the value of naming the enemy. It reallocates attention, access, and trust.

But the chapter will wreck a sloppy reader. Soraya feels public criticism in studio and wants an enemy story because enemy stories reduce ambiguity fast. Yet the incentive structure still binds the two students to a shared outcome. If she forces the war frame there, she burns a useful ally and weakens herself. Anxiety is eager to promote tension into hostility. The chapter only works if you refuse that promotion unless the structure actually supports it.

So the hard test is evidence. Who gains if you slip? What repeats? What happens if you cut access? Would this person's best outcome still require your competent success, or would your decline make their path easier? Those questions are colder than mood, and that is their value. They keep you from calling discomfort a threat while also keeping you from donating strength to a real opponent because the sharper label hurt your self-image.

Get the label wrong and the penalties split in opposite directions. Name opposition too late and the other side spends your innocence like capital. Name it too early and you wreck collaboration, shrink your network, and start fighting shadows. The chapter is the book's first demand for map accuracy. Chapter 2 raises the standard again by asking whether, after finally naming the rival correctly, you are still bringing yesterday's tactics into today's fight.

examples.title: Hugo Stops Sharing the Staffing Draft

scenario.gentle: Hugo manages a small analytics unit at a regional bank. A peer director keeps asking to see the draft staffing plan before the executive meeting, saying it will help the two teams stay aligned. Hugo has recently learned that the same director is arguing for a merged structure where Hugo would lose headcount and visibility.
scenario.direct: Hugo's peer wants early access to a staffing draft while privately backing a reorg that weakens Hugo's unit.
scenario.competitive: Hugo is being asked for the draft by the same director who gets bigger if Hugo gets smaller.

whatToDo.gentle: Stop treating the request as neutral. Share only the version that is ready for the common meeting, and route any private context through the executive sponsor whose incentives are not tied against you.
whatToDo.direct: Do not pre-brief the peer as if interests are shared. Tighten access and move sensitive context elsewhere instead.
whatToDo.competitive: Close the leak. No early draft for the person who profits from your narrowed scope.

whyItMatters.gentle: Once the incentive conflict is named, access has to change. Otherwise Hugo is funding the argument against himself.
whyItMatters.direct: The point is not rudeness. It is refusing to arm the other side with your own planning.
whyItMatters.competitive: A soft reading would turn Hugo's draft into the other director's ammunition.

scenario.gentle: Mireille works at a museum and has a cordial monthly check-in with a senior curator who keeps asking what she plans to propose at the next board review. She now knows his own expansion proposal is stronger if hers looks premature.

scenario.competitive: Mireille is being mined for board context by a man whose best outcome depends on her proposal dying quietly.

whatToDo.gentle: Mireille keeps the conversation polite but changes its content. She shares finished public facts, not tentative internal logic, and asks broader questions that reveal his position without feeding it.
whatToDo.direct: Keep the tone steady and stop supplying live context. Gather information; do not donate it.
whatToDo.competitive: Stay warm. Give nothing useful. Make the meeting informational, not confessional.

whyItMatters.gentle: The chapter's move is not a blowup. It is a cleaner trust map.
whyItMatters.direct: Once the relationship is classified correctly, disclosure rules have to change or the classification is meaningless.
whyItMatters.competitive: If Mireille keeps talking like interests are shared, the other curator leaves stronger every month.

examples.title: Elodie Predicts the Board Vote Before It Happens

scenario.gentle: Elodie serves on a volunteer arts board. One member keeps complimenting her energy while quietly asking others whether she has enough experience to lead next year's budget committee. Elodie has to decide whether this is ordinary caution or a real attempt to sideline her.
scenario.direct: A board member praises Elodie publicly and questions her readiness privately before a committee vote.
scenario.competitive: Elodie is being smiled at in public while her suitability is being negotiated downward in private.

whatToDo.gentle: Look for the structure before escalating. If the member's influence grows when Elodie is blocked, she should stop giving casual access and prepare her case with the full board instead.
whatToDo.direct: Test the incentives, then choose the tradeoff: preserve surface warmth or protect your position with tighter access and better preparation.
whatToDo.competitive: Read the gain map, then decide whether to keep buying warmth at the cost of being outmaneuvered.

whyItMatters.gentle: The tradeoff is real because early caution can feel harsh, but delayed caution can leave the room shaped without you.
whyItMatters.direct: Elodie is balancing relationship smoothness against preventable exposure.
whyItMatters.competitive: Wait too long and the vote is decided by a story you helped feed.

questions.prompt: Which definition fits the chapter's use of enemy?
choices: A person whose position improves when your position weakens
Any person who criticizes you in public
A rival who once beat you in a competition

explanation.gentle: The chapter uses a narrow structural definition, not a feeling-based one.
explanation.direct: Here the key is incentive structure, not irritation or embarrassment.
explanation.competitive: The real test is who profits when you lose ground.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter warn against confusing politeness with safety?
choices: Because rude people are usually easier to work with
Because opposed interests can still be expressed in calm language
Because polite people rarely tell the truth

explanation.gentle: A calm tone can coexist with a plan that still hurts your position.
explanation.direct: Notice what wins here: tone does not override the incentive map.
explanation.competitive: Soft speech can still carry a hard move.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main reversal?
choices: Enemy recognition should always lead to immediate confrontation
Readers should avoid all competition to stay fair
Treating everyone as an enemy turns the strategy into paranoia

explanation.gentle: The move breaks when the label spreads beyond evidence.
explanation.direct: The chapter draws a hard line against overapplication.
explanation.competitive: Call every hard room a war and your judgment is already slipping.

questions.prompt: Talia keeps seeing consolidation plans that leave the other division head stronger and her team smaller. Which detail most strongly supports naming real opposition?
choices: He sounds calm and institutionally minded in meetings
His proposal improves if her unit is absorbed
Other people in the room seem to like him

explanation.gentle: The relevant evidence is structural gain from Talia's reduced position.
explanation.direct: Talia's signal is the incentive pattern, not the meeting style.
explanation.competitive: If her contraction fattens his case, the map is already telling the truth.

questions.prompt: Hugo learns a peer director wants his staffing draft while backing a reorg that weakens Hugo's unit. What fits the chapter best?
choices: Stop pre-briefing the peer and route sensitive context elsewhere
Give the full draft anyway to prove good faith
Accuse the peer publicly before the executive meeting

explanation.gentle: The chapter changes disclosure rules before it demands open conflict.
explanation.direct: What makes that choice right is that it removes avoidable leakage without turning the room into theater.
explanation.competitive: The clean move is to shut the leak, not perform outrage.

questions.prompt: Kian and another doctoral student are finalists for one fellowship slot. The other finalist asks to exchange full proposal notes. What is the strongest response under this chapter?
choices: Trade everything because academic life should stay collaborative
Share broad themes but keep the private edge of the proposal to himself
Refuse all contact and insult the other finalist for asking

explanation.gentle: The chapter supports civility without naive overdisclosure in a real zero-sum setting.
explanation.direct: Kian's mistake would be treating a one-slot competition like a shared-build space.
explanation.competitive: One seat means you stay decent without handing over the blade.

questions.prompt: Soraya starts reading a studio classmate as hostile because the criticism is public and stressful. Which fact most clearly weakens the enemy reading?
choices: The classmate speaks bluntly in review
The classmate dresses more formally than Soraya
The project outcome still depends on both students succeeding together

explanation.gentle: Shared outcome is the clue that pressure has not yet become real opposition.
explanation.direct: Soraya's case shows why structural evidence matters more than emotional heat.
explanation.competitive: Joint outcome means the war story is probably your nerves talking.

questions.prompt: Elodie suspects a volunteer-board member is trying to sideline her. Before escalating, what evidence threshold fits the chapter best?
choices: Check whether the member's influence rises if Elodie loses the committee role
Assume hidden hostility because praise feels fake
Wait for a direct insult before changing anything

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants concrete incentive evidence before the label hardens.
explanation.direct: Evidence matters because mood is too unstable to carry the classification alone.
explanation.competitive: Read the gain map first, not the smile.

questions.prompt: Which cost is more likely when real opposition is named too late?
choices: You preserve every relationship and gain broad trust
You avoid leakage because the softer story keeps everyone calm
You donate timing, access, and context to someone using them against you

explanation.gentle: Late naming is costly because behavior stays soft while the other side keeps collecting advantage.
explanation.direct: Late naming hurts because the wrong disclosure pattern often stays in place the longest.
explanation.competitive: Call the room wrong and your own openness becomes enemy capital.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 2 logically build on this chapter?
choices: Once you name the enemy, the rest of the book is mostly repetition
Even after naming real opposition, you can still lose by using the last conflict's playbook on the current one
The next chapter argues that enemy recognition should usually be ignored

explanation.gentle: Chapter 1 fixes who the opponent is; Chapter 2 tests whether your reading of the situation is current.
explanation.direct: Even after naming the rival, you still need a live map of present conditions.
explanation.competitive: Correct target, dead playbook, same loss.

coreSkill.gentle: Core skill: classify real opposition by incentives instead of by emotion.
coreSkill.direct: Core skill: read the gain map before you decide who gets trust, access, and context.
coreSkill.competitive: Core skill: stop feeding people whose upside depends on your shrinkage.

plan.gentle: If a cordial colleague keeps asking for early drafts while their plan improves when my role shrinks, then I will stop private pre-briefing and document upward instead.
plan.direct: If a work relationship shows opposed incentives, then I will tighten access before the next meeting.
plan.competitive: If their win needs my loss, I close the leak immediately.

plan.gentle: If a school competition is truly one-slot or zero-sum, then I will stay civil without treating it like shared-build collaboration.
plan.direct: If the academic structure is competitive, then I will match my disclosure to that structure.
plan.competitive: If there is one seat, I stop pretending there are two winners.

plan.gentle: If a personal conflict feels total, then I will test whether the incentives are really opposed before I use enemy language.
plan.direct: If a personal relationship feels tense, then I will check for structural opposition before I escalate the frame.
plan.competitive: If it only feels bad but the outcome is still shared, I keep the war label off it.

twentyFourHourChallenge.gentle: Within 24 hours, map one live relationship under two headings: shared incentives and opposed incentives. Change one access habit based on the result.
twentyFourHourChallenge.direct: Today, run one relationship through an incentive audit and adjust one disclosure behavior.
twentyFourHourChallenge.competitive: Before tomorrow, find one leak created by a soft label and close it.

weeklyPractice.gentle: For one week, notice every time you feel tempted to call a conflict a misunderstanding. Ask what the incentive structure actually says before deciding.
weeklyPractice.direct: Spend seven days tracking one thing: where you soften or harden labels without enough evidence.
weeklyPractice.competitive: For a week, audit your conflict map and catch every fake ally or fake enemy before the room decides for you.

front.gentle: What turns a tense person into this chapter's definition of enemy?

back.gentle: Their position improves when yours weakens in a concrete way.
back.direct: Enemy status comes from opposed incentives, not from tone.

front.gentle: Why is politeness not enough evidence of safety?

back.gentle: A polite tone can still carry a pattern that weakens your position.
back.direct: Cordial presentation can mask real opposition.
back.competitive: Soft delivery can move a hard agenda.

front.gentle: What is the first behavioral change after real opposition is named?

back.gentle: You change access, disclosure, and timing.
back.direct: Tighten what you share before you escalate tone.
back.competitive: Shut the leak before the speech.

front.gentle: What does Soraya's studio case protect you from?
front.competitive: What fake story does pressure sell fast?

back.gentle: It warns that public tension can be misread as real opposition.
back.direct: Pressure can create false-enemy readings when incentives are still shared.

front.gentle: Which two costs must hard depth hold together?
front.direct: What are the two directions of error?
front.competitive: How can the map fail both ways?

back.gentle: Late naming leaves you exposed, and lazy naming poisons collaboration.
back.direct: Miss real opposition and you leak; invent it and you isolate yourself.
back.competitive: Too soft gets you used. Too hard leaves you alone.

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: Name real opposition by incentives, then guard your access without turning every hard relationship into a war.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: Read who benefits from your loss. That classification should change disclosure, not your appetite for drama.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: Map the gain line. Close the leak. Keep the label rare enough to stay sharp.
